input:
In this worked example, we will determine the volumetric flow rate of a viscous liquid flowing laminarly through a tube, making use of the well-known Hagen-Poiseuille equation. The liquid in question has a viscosity $\mu$ of 0.05 Pa s, and it flows through a tube having a radius $R$ of 6 mm and a length $L$ of 21 m. The pressure drop $\Delta P$ that drives the flow amounts to 20 kPa. The Hagen-Poiseuille equation, which relates the volumetric flow $Q$ to precisely these quantities, is written as follows:

$$Q = \frac{\pi R^4 \Delta P}{8 \mu L}$$

It is important to note that this elegant equation rests upon a number of underlying assumptions: it assumes that the flow is laminar in character, that it is fully developed along the length of the tube, and that the liquid in question behaves as a Newtonian fluid. When the values set out above are substituted into the equation, the volumetric flow $Q$ comes out at 34.9 L h-1. This result should, of course, be interpreted in the light of the assumptions that have just been mentioned, since any departure from the laminar regime, or any non-Newtonian behaviour on the part of the liquid, would mean that the relationship embodied in the equation no longer provides a dependable description of the flow, and an alternative approach would then have to be sought.
target:
The task is to determine the volumetric flow of a viscous liquid in laminar flow through a tube. The liquid has a viscosity $\mu$ of 0.05 Pa s; the tube has a radius $R$ of 6 mm and a length $L$ of 21 m; the pressure drop $\Delta P$ along the tube is 20 kPa. The flow is taken as laminar and fully developed, and the liquid as Newtonian. Under those conditions the Hagen-Poiseuille equation holds for the flow and gives the volumetric flow $Q$ from the radius, the pressure drop, the viscosity and the length by

$$Q = \frac{\pi R^4 \Delta P}{8 \mu L}$$

Substitution of the stated values in the equation gives $Q$ as 34.9 L h-1. The check on the result is the regime: the value is the flow that the stated pressure drop maintains while the flow stays laminar and fully developed in a Newtonian liquid. A flow outside the laminar regime is outside the equation, and the equation states no value for it; the result therefore stands or falls with the regime, not with the arithmetic, which the stated values fix completely. The stated values are also the whole of the data the example uses — the geometry of the tube, the property of the liquid and the driving pressure drop — and no other quantity is needed by the relation or admitted into the result.
